view: الصرام means date harvesting, from a root meaning cutting; صرم and صريمة refer to separation and to a broken-off sand tract, as illustrated by poems including one of Imru al-Qays.
note: This lexical explanation concerns the following verse's wording.

view: Other forms of the same cutting root describe a decisive cutter, a she-camel whose milk has stopped, a month or year nearing its end, and a person whose fortune has turned bad.
note: This lexical explanation concerns the following verse's wording.

view: الصريم can describe trees stripped of fruit.
note: Tabatabai describes cut, fruitless trees; the word appears in the following verse.

view: الصريم can mean night, day, or dawn; al-Shammir explains night and day as opposites named because each parts from the other.
note: Ibn Abbas compares the ruined garden to black night; the word appears in the following verse.

view: Ibn Abbas says الصريم means ash in the language of Khuzaima.
note: This explanation concerns the following verse's wording.

view: الصريم can describe a known barren sand tract in Yemen.
note: This explanation concerns the following verse's wording.

view: A Prophetic report applies the warning that sin can withhold prepared provision to the owners' loss of their crop.
note: One version also says sin can cause lost knowledge and missed night prayer.

view: Accounts describe the garden as belonging to a righteous man who left it to his family and town, and variously place it near Sana'a in Yemen, in Abyssinia, or among the People of Scripture.
note: These are reported elaborations of the story.

view: The garden's loss may be punishment or a trial serving as grace, because it brought its owners to repentance.
note: The two accounts differ in how they characterize the disaster.

view: Their refusal to help the poor caused the garden's loss; at first the sons thought they had lost their way, then recognized the consequence of their refusal.
The owners' firm resolve and oath to withhold charity made them culpable before they carried out the refusal.
The garden became like dry harvested stubble after the visitation.
note: Ibn Kathir attributes the stubble explanation to al-Thawri and al-Suddi.

view: The passage admonishes people who do not share their wealth, but its worldly punishment does not establish that the owners withheld obligatory zakat.
The parable addresses people who call the Prophet possessed and feel secure: divine punishment can ruin plans fixed by pledges just as people wake to carry them out.
The affliction descended upon and encircled the whole orchard.
note: The accounts describe the calamity as surrounding the garden on every side.

view: The root ṭawf means circling around something; al-Raghib explains guarding by circling and extensions to a night visitor, jinn, an image, and a servant.
note: Ibn Ashur says the literal action is walking around something.

view: With the preposition على, طاف conveys taking control of or descending upon the garden.
The image of circling portrays a calamity reaching the entire garden, like the specter mentioned at 7:201.
The pronoun refers to the orchard.
A طائف is an event or visitation that comes at night; on this reading the word itself marks the calamity as nocturnal.
note: Al-Farra is repeatedly named for this restriction. Other notes challenge it by citing 7:201.

view: Arab usage can explicitly speak of visiting by day, despite the ordinary night sense; Abu al-Jarrah's poem gives an example, and al-Farra cites a daytime expression for something unexpected or impossible.
The word need not be restricted to night, since 7:201 uses طائف for Satan's touch without specifying nighttime.
note: These authors object to or reject al-Farra's nighttime restriction.

view: طائف can mean a calamity or destructive occurrence and generally suggests harm.
note: Alusi reports Ibn Abbas calling it an event and Qatada calling it punishment.

view: Al-Farra associates طائف with a dream specter, but Ibn Ashur questions deriving it from a portion of the night.
The kind of calamity is left unnamed because its effect matters more than its type; assigning the action to an unspecified visitor functions like a passive construction.
The indefinite طائف magnifies the event, which the next verse reveals as a ruinous calamity.
Al-Nakhaʿi read طيف in place of طائف.
note: Samin notes that the pair was discussed at 7:201.

view: The visitor was a divine punishment or scourge that struck the garden.
note: The notes also give God's command or a fiery agent as descriptions of the visitor.

view: The visitor was an act, event, decree, or command from God.
note: Several reports ascribe this explanation to Ibn Abbas; Qatada calls it God's command or punishment.

view: The visitor was fire sent from heaven or by God, which burned the garden and its crops.
note: Ibn Abbas's account says the fire surrounded the orchard; one report says it blackened it.

view: One report identifies the visitor as Satan.
note: Another report there identifies Gabriel instead.

view: A neck, tongue, or mass of fire issued from the garden's valley, described in some reports as a valley of Hell, and destroyed it.
note: The report is attributed to Ibn Jurayj; one account says the fire burned the garden to its roots.

view: Gabriel uprooted the orchard, carried it around the Kaaba, and planted it at the site of Taif, explaining the town's name and its water, trees, and grapes.
note: Alusi rejects the relocation story and related versions as unsound.

view: The night visitor burned the garden; its destructive agency is described as fire or as some other agent.
note: The explanation leaves the precise agent open.

view: The phrase من ربك may attach to the verb طاف or function as an adjective qualifying طائف.
Attributing the disaster to God signals how unexpectedly and instantly the orchard was devastated.
note: Islahi describes the devastation as miraculous, reducing the orchard to nothing in a blink.

view: The affliction originated from God and was sent by Him as punishment for failing to give thanks.
note: Ibn Ashur names ingratitude as the reason for the destruction.

view: The words reassure the Prophet amid Quraysh's apparent ease: God can suddenly destroy such security.
The destroying visitor was a slight act for God though devastating to the orchard; calling it from your Lord frames the punishment as merciful correction intended to reform the Prophet's people.
The phrase وهم نائمون is a circumstantial clause: the owners were asleep when the garden was struck.
note: The sleep places the event at night.

view: If طائف already implies nighttime, the mention of the owners sleeping reinforces that sense and depicts the scene.
The owners were heedless of the decree that had reached their orchard.
note: Alusi records this as an alternative to literal sleep and prefers literal sleeping at night in context.

view: The owners were literally sleeping at night when the calamity struck; the surrounding verses favor this reading.
note: Alusi explicitly prefers the literal sense over the heedlessness explanation.

view: Sleep is a light death, and death is a heavy sleep.
